extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent applicants, and patent attorneys working on pharmaceuticals, food, functional water, and chemical compound inventions
extracted.subtask_description: Examination guidelines for patentability, description and claim requirements, and unpatentability considerations for inventions in pharmaceuticals (dosage regimens), food (sensory/functional), functional drinking water, and chemical compounds (including polymorphs and inorganic microstructure).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step for dosage regimen/dose
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive step may be acknowledged only for a specific dosage regimen and dose which are deemed to be worthwhile to be protected as a patent due to prominent or heterogeneous effect for which a person skilled in the art cannot expect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claimed dosage/regimen in light of closest prior art; inventive step requires an unexpected/prominent or qualitatively heterogeneous effect not predictable from prior art. Examples: (Ex1) small once-daily 1 mg dose refused where prior art taught 0.5–2.5 mg and predicted valid effect; (Ex2) monthly high-dose (150 mg) could be inventive if it shows unexpectedly striking differences (e.g., bone density improvement) that are not predictable merely because higher dose often increases bioavailability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability/obviousness of dosage optimizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Optimization of unit administration volume and administration method is a general technical issue in the medical field and may be predictable to a person skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If closest prior art suggests range or alludes to administration conveniences, selecting a particular dose/regimen within expected optimization may be obvious. Examiners should assess whether claimed benefits are predictable or genuinely unexpected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step for polymorphic/crystalline forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention of crystal with claims stating compounds of specific crystal having different form of crystal from the compound in cited document is deemed to have the inventive step if it has different effect qualitatively or quantitatively with the compound in cited document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that different polymorphs can affect solubility, safety, stability, etc.; inventive step is present if the new crystal form exhibits qualitatively different effects or substantially different quantitative effects. The effect should be stated in the specification; if doubtful, prove by submitting trusted documents (e.g., comparative studies) after filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to state effect of polymorph in description
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of a claimed polymorphic crystal form should be stated in the description of the crystal form invention, not merely reported by comparison with cited documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If effect is doubtful, applicants should provide proof (comparative studies, trusted documents). Lack of clear statement/proof can lead to refusal on inventive-step grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to evaluate food inventions for public safety
rubrics_metrics.description: In examining an invention directed to food, it is necessary to determine whether the food is harmful to the health of the public, and unique matters including how to describe sensory effects and functional effects of a healthy food should be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Food is readily accessible and ingested repeatedly; examiners must scrutinize safety and whether description/claims appropriately limit intended use. Food taken as medicine is excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory effect of food must be proven objectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensory quality (taste, smell, appearance, texture, etc.) cannot be determined solely by personal sense of an inventor; it is necessary to prove its effect objectively and scientifically through physiochemical or mechanical analysis, or systemic sensory test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific methods, devices, and requirements in the description so a skilled person can reproduce the analysis. Use instrument-based measurements or standardized sensory tests when instrument correlation is weak or complexity requires human panels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiochemical/mechanical analysis requirements for sensory features
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods, devices, requirements, etc. for physiochemical or mechanical analysis should be stated specifically in the description to support the sensory feature according to analysis results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of analysis devices: colorimeter/spectrophotometer (color), GC/electronic nose (scent), electronic tongue/refractometer/pH meter (flavor), viscometer/texture analyzer/rheometer/amylograph (viscosity/texture). Include sufficient detail so results support claimed sensory features (example: Brix change measured by refractometer to support increased sweetness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensory test method and reporting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: When sensory tests are used, the method of the sensory test, number and selection standards of panels, and results should be stated with quantity and detailed description to objectively support effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trained panels if appropriate, describe test protocol, selection criteria, statistical analysis, and present quantitative results that allow distinguishing effects (example: mix of monosodium glutamate and X shown distinguishable by trained panels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional effect of food must be scientifically supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional effects (e.g., health improvement, disease prevention) shall be stated in detail and clearly confirmed by experiments in vitro, animal testing, clinical tests, or biomarkers which can support effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If effective dose of a functional raw material is publicly known and sufficient to identify function, repeating proof may be unnecessary. Otherwise provide objective experimental evidence. If content of active ingredient is minimal, description deficiency may be ground for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of publicly known functional raw material
rubrics_metrics.description: If effective dose of a functional raw material or ingredient is publicly known and sufficient to identify its function, a mixture including it may be deemed to include the effect without re-proving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define 'functional raw material publicly known' (e.g., declared by Minister, separately recognized raw materials, or functions published domestically/internationally). Ensure the known effective dose is clearly relevant to the claimed composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims: usage limiting a health functional food is a claim element
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject matter recited in a claim is a health functional food, the usage limiting the food is considered as a claim element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that usage limitations may be interpreted as claim elements; but a mere different usage does not necessarily guarantee novelty if composition is identical to prior art (see Supreme Court precedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims of use must be expressed by objectives, not by quality
rubrics_metrics.description: For a use invention of a health functional food, its usage shall be specifically described by objectives to be achieved through the quality, not by the quality itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'for improvement of hyperlipidemia', 'for drop in blood sugar' are acceptable objective-style usage descriptions. Avoid limitiations stated as 'quality' (e.g., 'having activating antagonism for binding receptor') which specify function/mechanism rather than an intended use and may not be construed as a use invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between food-usage and medicinal-use claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Health functional food usage may be stated in terms of types of function helpful to the human body, but food claims should not be drafted as medicinal treatment claims (e.g., 'to treat taurine deficiency disease' is unclear for food).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that effectively claim therapeutic treatment may be deemed unclear or inappropriate for food; draft usage limitations consistent with food (general functional benefits) rather than medical treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Food unpatentability due to safety concerns (Article 32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Food shall be safe for human body; where safety of food material or its compound is not clear to a person skilled in the art, the invention is deemed harmful to public health and examiner shall notify grounds for rejection under Article 32.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess safety including secondary products from storage/processing. If safety is uncertain, require submission of safety test reports or objective documents. Examples of problematic cases include new materials never consumed as food, materials prohibited by government reports, materials with reported harmfulness in journals, or descriptions of intake beyond scientific knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to safety objections and risk of new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may respond to safety objections by submitting objective documents to prove safety; however, adding explanations and documents on safety in an amendment may be considered an addition of new matter if not clearly recognizable from the original specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should be cautious when supplementing safety data post-filing; if safety evidence was not supported by the original disclosure, amendments may introduce unallowable new matter (see Guidelines Part IV Chapter 2 re new matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination when both food and pharmaceutical claims filed
rubrics_metrics.description: If both health functional food and medicinal product are filed in one application, it shall be determined separately whether each can be harmful to public health.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For pharmaceutical composition claims examine per medicinal guidelines; for food composition consider food safety. A compound with great effect may still be unpatentable as food if harmful to humans even though patentable as a pharmaceutical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional drinking water: need for objective proof of claimed properties
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions of functional drinking water (e.g., electrolyzed reduced water, hexagonal water, magnetized water), it is necessary to satisfy description requirements including statement of medical effect, statement of maintaining magnetic state, and to submit objective tests/measuring methods when not acceptable as common technical knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims are limited to parameters like pH, ORP, active hydrogen, etc., the process and beneficial effects must be stated and supported; where assertions are not consistent with common technical knowledge, reliable test results must be submitted. Notes caution against unsupported theories (e.g., pyramid-produced hexagonal water) without scientific proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industrial applicability and 'uncompleted invention' in functional water
rubrics_metrics.description: A manufacturing device or method for producing a claimed functional water without test reports/evidence that the water is actually produced is considered an uncompleted invention which is impossible to accomplish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not accept purely theoretical processes or empirical rules without scientific proof. Require evidence that the claimed product can be made and has the claimed properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: General principle: inventions harmful to public hygiene unpatentable
rubrics_metrics.description: If an invention intends to disrupt public order/faith or be harmful to public health, patent shall not be granted; for manufacturing processes consider both the process and its result for public hygiene impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If beneficial inventions may be possibly harmful, examine measures to remove harmful parts or perform benefit-risk comparisons. Do not deem an invention unpatentable solely because it exceeds water quality standards without further evidence; if safety is proved with objective documents it can be patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical compound: requirement for characterization data and synthetic procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirmatory data to identify compounds and the preparation (synthetic procedure) shall be stated in the description of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If it's doubtful that the compound can be produced from the disclosed preparation (e.g., complex process or undesired side reactions), provide characterization data such as elemental analysis, NMR, melting/boiling point. For polymorphs provide XRD, DSC, IR and/or chemical/physical data. Preparation method must be clearly stated unless a skilled person could prepare the compound from the disclosure and the art's skill level at filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical compound: disclosure of representative embodiments for generic claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For inventions relating to a new chemical compound, embodiment specifying technical means shall be disclosed. Where the claim is recited generically, representative embodiment(s) shall be disclosed by a group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no representative embodiments are provided for a Markush/genus-type claim and a skilled person cannot recognize other species, examiner shall notify lack of support. Provide representative examples across the claimed scope when claiming classes of compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be supported by the description
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim (e.g., Markush-type compound group) is not clearly supported by the description so a person skilled in the art can recognize the claimed members, the examiner shall present grounds for rejection for lack of support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide reasons when rejecting and consider amendment to description or claims to align scope with disclosed embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity requirements for chemical compound claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If a chemical compound is specified by name or structural formula the claim is clear; if necessary, physical/chemical property or preparation can be used to define the invention. Expressions like 'alkyl' or 'aryl' without carbon number may be acceptable if the variety can be introduced based on the chemical framework, but unspecified 'substituted …' or vague terms like 'derivative'/'homologous series' must clearly identify scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether unspecified substituents or vague group terms render the invention unsupported or not reproducible; specify carbon numbers or embodiments where necessary to preserve clarity and enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty: compound defined by characteristics, salts, purity
rubrics_metrics.description: A compound defined by specific characteristics that is identical to a well-known compound specified by name or structural formula lacks novelty. A known compound's conventional salt is substantially identical and lacks novelty. Simple purity improvement of a known compound lacks novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claimed compound is distinguishable by distinct natural properties beyond mere purity or salt form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty rules for preparation/method claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claimed preparation method is the same as prior art and merely limited by use, it is deemed to lack novelty. If the claimed preparation uses starting material produced by a particular preparation but other conditions are equivalent to prior art, the claimed preparation may lack novelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine method claims for whether they produce a substantially same compound or rely on different, non-obvious process steps; use limitations alone are insufficient to establish novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step for chemical compounds: structure and special effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventive step of a chemical compound invention is determined by two features: (i) structural formula and (ii) technically special effect of the chemical compound. Improved/unexpected effects compared to prior art are very important especially where effects are hard to predict from structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not deny inventive step solely because of similar structure; unexpected technical advantages (final result, chemical feature, purpose/use) support inventive step. Conversely, if invention was easily arrived at by a skilled person, inventive step may be denied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step for crystalline/polymorphic forms (chemical compounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new crystal form of a known chemical compound is considered to have inventive step if its effect is qualitatively different or substantially quantitatively different from the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects should be stated clearly in the description even if no comparative test data vs prior art are given; if effects are doubtful, provide concrete evidence such as comparative test data trusted by applicant/patentee (see Supreme Court precedent).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inorganic compound inventions: microstructure and property specification
rubrics_metrics.description: For inorganic compounds, even with same name/formula, physical properties or configuration including microstructure (crystal form, unit surface area of particles, etc.) can differ; subject matter may not be specified by name/formula alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should include specific properties to enable identification of microstructure; determine whether the specific property can be expected to result from the claimed adoption/combination of components given the level of technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-use (use-limited product) claim construction and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: When a chemical compound is claimed with a 'for ~' use limitation (e.g., 'Compound Z for Y'), the limitation may be construed as indication of utility only and the claim read as the compound without use limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, a use-limited product claim may lack novelty if the compound itself is disclosed in prior art. Drafters should consider alternative claim formats (e.g., second medical use-style claims where permissible) to capture new therapeutic uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection invention inventive step requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For a selection invention to be novel over a prior art generic disclosure and to have inventive step, the selected species should have different effect from that of the prior art invention qualitatively or quantitatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely selecting specific compounds from a wide known genus without demonstrating distinct effects will likely lack inventive step. Provide data demonstrating unique properties or advantages for the selected species.
